stem: For a positive integer n, let P(n)=n(n+1)(n+2) and Q(n)=n(n+1)(n+2)(n+3). A learner knows that P(n) is always divisible by 6, and makes two further claims: (A) P(n) is divisible by 12 for every n; (B) Q(n) is divisible by 24 for every n. For each claim decide whether it holds for every positive n and give a proof or a counterexample. If a claim fails, determine exactly which positive starting n make it true, and prove your classification. Explain why knowing that a product is divisible by 6 does not by itself establish divisibility by 12. Do not rely on checking finitely many starting values to prove a universal statement.
conditions: n is an arbitrary positive integer
the 6-divisibility of a three-integer product is a given starting fact
a counterexample may disprove 'every', but does not classify all successful n
classification must be proved across every possible positive n

a_general_warrant: Three consecutive integers always supply a factor of 3.
When n ≡ 1 (mod 4), the only even member is n+1, which is ≡2 (mod 4), so the triple has just one factor of two and is not divisible by 4.
When n ≡ 0 or 3 (mod 4), one member is divisible by 4. When n ≡ 2 (mod 4), two members are even and one is divisible by 4. Thus in all three classes n ≠1 mod4, the triple has a factor of 4.
Since 3 divides the triple for all n and gcd(3,4)=1, divisibility by 12 holds precisely outside n ≡1 mod4.
b_general_warrant: Among four consecutive integers one is divisible by 4 and a distinct integer two steps away from it is even.
The product therefore has at least three factors of 2, meaning 8 divides Q(n) for every n.
Among any three consecutive integers one is divisible by 3, hence 3 divides Q(n) for every n.
Since gcd(8,3)=1, 24 divides Q(n) for every positive n.
answer_for_review_only.independent_modular_check: As a falsifier, check all n modulo 24 for Q and all n modulo 12 for P. These finite *complete residue classes* cover every n by polynomial congruence; they are not merely sample starts.
answer_for_review_only.crux: A universal 6-divisibility proof does not supply sufficient powers of two for 12 or 24; locate and justify the extra powers, including the distinct even factors within four consecutive integers.
